title: Richard Allen (1794)
hookLine: pulled from his knees in a segregated church, he founds the African Methodist Episcopal Church

lines: ON THEIR KNEES IN THE GALLERY.
A HAND PULLS ABSALOM JONES UP.
cards: Sunday morning in Philadelphia. The prayer has already begun, and a group of Black Methodists are on their knees in the gallery of a church they had given money to finish.

Then a hand grabs one of them, a man named Absalom Jones, and tries to haul him to his feet. A church officer is telling him he's kneeling in the wrong place. Jones asks to be allowed to finish praying first.
The officer won't wait. Kneeling nearby, a preacher who had once been enslaved sees all of it.

teach.b: We have this story in Allen's own words. He wrote an account of his life, plain and unshowy. He was born enslaved and came to faith among the Methodists.
His account says the man who held him in slavery heard a Methodist preacher, came to believe slavery was wrong, and agreed to let Allen buy his freedom. Allen worked, paid, and was free.
He preached in Philadelphia, and Black worshipers came to hear him in growing numbers. Then came that Sunday.

teach.h: PULLED UP IN THE MIDDLE OF PRAYER.
teach.b: They were told to sit in the gallery, and when they knelt in what they thought was the right place, an officer pulled Jones up off his knees in the middle of the prayer.

teach.h: WE ALL WENT OUT IN A BODY.
teach.b: When the prayer ended, Allen writes, "we all went out of the church in a body". They didn't stay to argue. They didn't burn anything down.
They walked out together. And then they built.
Allen's account tells of buying an old blacksmith's shop, hauling it onto a lot, and fitting it out as a place to worship. It was called Bethel, the house of God.
Out of it grew the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and Allen became its bishop.
Paul wrote to the Galatians: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."
Allen's church didn't walk away from Methodism or from that verse. It walked away from a gallery, and built a house where nobody would be pulled off their knees.

how: The African Methodist Episcopal Church remembers Richard Allen as its founder, and Mother Bethel in Philadelphia still gathers for worship on the same ground.

games.q: you're kneeling in prayer, and a church officer pulls your friend up off his knees. what do you do?
o: shout back and start a fight in the church.
finish the prayer, then walk out together.
move quietly to the gallery and say nothing.
games.why: Jones asked to finish praying. when the prayer ended, Allen writes, we all went out of the church in a body, and then they built Bethel.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and bring to mind someone who has been left out lately: at work, at school, in a family, a group chat or a church.

Picture them a little outside the circle, then picture yourself walking over and standing next to them, not fixing anything, just there. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, keep them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Richard Allen. A preacher born enslaved who bought his freedom, walked out of a segregated church with his people, and helped found the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

carryVoice: Your line: we all went out. Out of a gallery, into a house of their own. That's nine hundred eleven.
